summary:
Strelka is a daily health check-in app for astronauts, built for the challenge Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions. On deep-space missions, a reply from Earth can take up to 48 minutes, so crews need to spot health problems early and act on their own.

Each day, astronauts log their vitals, sleep, mood, stress, exercise and symptoms in about two minutes. They can type the answers or say them out loud. Strelka compares each reading with that astronaut's own normal, taken from their pre-flight numbers or learned from their first week of check-ins. This catches slow drifts that happen in space before they leave textbook ranges. Every check-in ends with one of four plain answers: all good, keep an eye on it, tell your crew medic, or get help now. The advice also depends on how far the crew is from Earth, so on the way to Mars it says to start the onboard steps first.

An interactive body map links each reading to NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight. The app works fully offline on the web and as a desktop app. It helps crews stay healthy and make good decisions without depending on mission control.
details:
What it does and how it works

Strelka is a health check-in app for astronauts on long missions. It is named after Strelka, one of the dogs that orbited Earth on Sputnik 5 in 1960 and returned healthy.

There are check-ins in the morning, afternoon and before sleep. Astronauts log heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen, temperature, glucose, sleep, mood, stress, exercise and symptoms. They can type the answers or fill in the form by voice. Each field shows right away if a value looks off, and a "how do I measure this?" guide explains each reading.

Strelka compares each reading with the astronaut's own normal, not only textbook ranges. Their normal comes from pre-flight numbers they enter, or from the average of their first seven check-ins. The app then looks for three things:

Single readings that are outside safe limits or have drifted too far from the astronaut's normal.

Trends: a reading that has been off on each of the last three check-ins.

Combinations that point to known spaceflight conditions. For example, headache plus a vision change, or rising blood pressure, can be a sign of SANS (Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome).

Each day ends with one of four plain answers: All good, Keep an eye on it, Tell your crew medic, or Get help now. Each answer comes with clear next steps. The advice also depends on the mission. On the ISS the ground can answer almost instantly. On a Mars transit a reply can take up to 48 minutes round trip, so Strelka tells the crew to start the onboard steps first.

Other features:

An interactive body map links each reading to NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight and to related NASA research.

A history page where every check-in can be opened, edited or deleted, and missed days can be added.

A downloadable report for the crew medic.

A guided breathing break that is suggested when stress is high.

A demo mode with 180 days of made-up Mars transit data.

Benefits and intended impact

On deep-space missions, crews can't count on mission control in real time. Strelka helps them notice problems early and decide for themselves when to act. Because readings are judged against each person's own normal, it can catch slow changes before they leave the "healthy" range. It turns raw numbers into a clear decision, so the crew doesn't need medical training to know what to do next. The same approach could help people in remote or isolated places on Earth, such as polar stations, ships or rural areas.

Tools and technologies

Languages: JavaScript (JSX), HTML, CSS

Frontend: React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts for charts, Phosphor Icons

Voice: Web Speech API for speech recognition, with our own parser that turns spoken answers into form values

Desktop: Electron, packaged with electron-builder for Windows and macOS

Testing: Vitest for the triage, scheduling, streak and voice-parsing logic

Deployment: Docker, nginx and Cloudflare Tunnel, hosted at strelka.health

Data: Everything is stored on the device, so the app works fully offline. No special hardware is needed.

What makes it creative

It compares each astronaut with their own normal, not with an average person on Earth.

It changes its advice based on the distance to Earth.

It spots combinations of symptoms that relate to real spaceflight risks like SANS.

Hands-free voice check-ins fit how astronauts work, often with their hands busy.

What our team considered

Communication delay: the app must help even when the ground is far away.

Offline use: there is no reliable internet in space, so nothing depends on a server.

Speed: a check-in takes about two minutes and fits into a busy crew schedule.

Clarity: plain language and four simple answers instead of medical jargon.

NASA sources: the hazards and risks follow NASA's Human Research Program, and the readings reflect studies like NASA's Standard Measures and ARCHeR on Artemis II.

Safety and honesty: Strelka is a prototype, not a medical device. Its role is to support the crew medic, not replace them.
